title: Project activities
body_markdown:
## Project activities

The August 2025 Richfield planning study evaluated six concept-level flood-risk mitigation options at Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace. The concept-level construction estimates are expressed in 2025 U.S. dollars, have an estimated accuracy range of -30% to +50%, and exclude planning, engineering and design, construction management, permitting, property or easement acquisition, escalation, operations and maintenance, and monitoring.

[Information needed: Confirm which flood-risk mitigation concept this Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application will fund.]

### Available concept-level activities and quantifiable outputs

| Location and concept | Concept-level activities | Quantifiable output | Planning-level construction cost estimate |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Wilson Pond Concept A | Lower the water level in Wilson Pond ahead of a storm event through a remotely accessed gate controlled by weather forecasts; lower outlet and downstream storm sewer inverts; and increase storm sewer capacity from Wilson Pond toward Highway 494. | Approximately 5 acre-feet of additional Wilson Pond storage ahead of a storm event, assuming a 24-hour drawdown period. | $8,853,000 ($6,198,000–$15,493,000) |
| Wilson Pond Concept B | Replace the downstream storm sewer from Wilson Pond to Highway 494 with a single box culvert. | One 5-foot by 5-foot box culvert; the existing circular pipe ranges from 2.5 to 4.5 feet in diameter. | $11,536,000 ($8,076,000–$20,188,000) |
| Wilson Pond Concept C | Increase the number and size of downstream storm sewer pipes from Wilson Pond to Highway 494. | Two parallel 5-foot by 5-foot box culverts. | $17,333,000 ($12,134,000–$30,333,000) |
| Northwest of Roosevelt Park Concept A | Construct an underground storage chamber beneath the Roosevelt Park baseball fields; divert surface drainage from Roosevelt Park and along 76th Street; and modify storm sewer connections. | Approximately 354,000 cubic feet of underground water-retention storage, based on a 300-foot by 300-foot surface area, 5.25-foot depth, and 75% stormwater-storage availability. | $15,491,000 ($10,844,000–$27,110,000) |
| Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept A | Construct an underground storage chamber under the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments; regrade the parking lot; and modify storm sewer connections. | Approximately 24,000 cubic feet of underground water-retention storage, based on an approximately 8,000-square-foot surface area, 3-foot depth, and 75% stormwater-storage availability. | $1,540,000 ($1,078,000–$2,695,000) |
| Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept B | Increase storm sewer capacity from the northwest corner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments to Wood Lake. | Increase pipe diameters from a current range of 3 to 4 feet to a range of 3 to 6 feet. | $7,440,000 ($5,208,000–$13,020,000) |

### Concept-level implementation considerations

The Wilson Pond concepts would increase the volume and peak discharge rate leaving the Richfield municipal boundary. They assume that additional flow can be routed from Highway 494 through the City of Bloomington or along the Highway 494 corridor to the Minnesota River; this routing is not included in the planning-level cost estimates and would require further coordination and permitting discussions.

The Northwest of Roosevelt Park concept includes an outlet control structure to retain water during a storm while allowing the underground storage to drain after the event. The Near Woodlawn Terrace underground-storage concept would require an agreement with the owner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments.

All six alternatives remain concept-level designs. Further evaluation is identified as necessary for design optimization, utility conflicts, permitting requirements, applicable agreements with private landowners or other public entities, and project-specific design considerations.

title: Summary of flood damages
body_markdown:
## Summary of flood damages

The August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Prioritization* study provides modeled inundation evidence for flood-risk areas in Richfield. It does not document observed flood-damage claims, repair costs, or structure-specific damage inspections. The project for which funding is sought has not yet been identified; consequently, the damages summary below describes the locations evaluated in the planning study rather than the impacts associated with a selected grant project.

[Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept for which this Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application will summarize flood damages.]

### Flooding and inundation evidence

The updated PCSWMM model simulated four 24-hour design rainfall events: Atlas 14 2-year (2.83 inches), 10-year (4.24 inches), and 100-year (7.50 inches) events, plus a Mid-21st century 100-year moderate rainfall estimate (MCE100-year) event of 10.20 inches. The MCE100-year event was included to estimate long-term extreme-weather trends relevant to flood mitigation.

Model peak water levels for the four events were used to delineate inundation areas in ponds, wetlands, and topographic depressions. The study notes that this level-pool mapping did not map sloped water surfaces along roadways or through floodplains. The available inundation maps are Figure 3-1 (2-year event), Figure 3-2 (10-year event), Figure 3-3 (100-year event), and Figure 3-4 (MCE100-year event) of the August 2025 study.

The prioritization evaluated 746 flood-risk areas across the study area, of which 601 were located within or primarily within the Richfield municipal boundary. It considered storm-system conditions, critical infrastructure, frequency of flooding, social vulnerability index, and the number of potentially flood-prone structures.

### Severity at locations evaluated for mitigation

City staff identified three locations for planning-level evaluation:

- **Wilson Pond:** The study identifies the area as one of the locations with the largest flood risk in Richfield. It impacts the most residential structures in a single location; the lowest structures are affected during the 2-year, 24-hour rainfall event. Wilson Pond is within an area with a high social vulnerability index, and modeled surface inundation affects a critical transportation route and a school.
- **Northwest of Roosevelt Park:** The flood-risk area affects multiple structures in one location, with the lowest structures affected during the 10-year, 24-hour rainfall event. It is within an area with a high social vulnerability index, and modeled surface inundation affects a critical transportation route.
- **Near Woodlawn Terrace:** The flood-risk area affects multiple structures in one location, with the lowest structures affected during the 2-year, 24-hour rainfall event. Storm sewer pipes are classified as moderate to high risk; the area is within an area with a high social vulnerability index; and modeled surface inundation affects three high-density housing structures.

These findings are model-based indicators of potential inundation and exposure. They should not be presented as records of observed damage without supporting documentation.

[Information needed: Provide documented flood-damage records for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project area.]

### Available maps and supporting documentation

The August 2025 study includes citywide inundation maps for the 2-year, 10-year, 100-year, and MCE100-year 24-hour storm events, as well as concept-level maps comparing existing and modeled mitigation conditions at Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace. These materials document modeled conditions evaluated in the August 2025 study.

[Information needed: Provide photographs documenting flooding in the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project area.]

### Presidential disaster declarations

The available planning study does not identify county-level presidential disaster declarations associated with flooding in the proposed project area.

[Information needed: Confirm the county presidential disaster declaration number relevant to flooding in the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project area, or confirm that none applies.]

title: Project description
body_markdown:
## Project description

The City of Richfield's August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Prioritization* study updated the City's hydrologic and hydraulic stormwater model, evaluated flood-risk areas using environmental-justice and other factors, and modeled concept-level flood-risk-reduction alternatives at three locations. The study identified six concepts at Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace. It states that additional design and evaluation are required before the City pursues a mitigation project.

[Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept that this Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application will fund.]

### Immediate-phase objective and scope

The immediate-phase objective and activities cannot be confirmed until the grant-funded concept and current project phase are identified. The available study provides concept-level alternatives rather than a selected project scope.

[Information needed: Confirm the activities that the current phase of the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project will fund.]

### Available concept-level alternatives

The August 2025 study evaluated the following potential flood-risk-reduction concepts:

- **Wilson Pond Concept A:** Lower the Wilson Pond water level ahead of a storm event using a remotely accessed gate controlled by weather forecasts; lower outlet and downstream storm-sewer inverts; and increase storm-sewer capacity from Wilson Pond toward Highway 494.
- **Wilson Pond Concept B:** Increase storm-sewer capacity from Wilson Pond to Highway 494 through a single 5-foot-by-5-foot box culvert.
- **Wilson Pond Concept C:** Increase the number and size of storm-sewer pipes from Wilson Pond to Highway 494 through two parallel 5-foot-by-5-foot box culverts.
- **Northwest of Roosevelt Park Concept A:** Construct an underground storage chamber beneath the Roosevelt Park baseball fields, divert surface drainage from Roosevelt Park and along 76th Street, and modify storm-sewer connections.
- **Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept A:** Construct an underground storage chamber beneath the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments, regrade the parking lot, and modify storm-sewer connections.
- **Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept B:** Increase storm-sewer capacity from the northwest corner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments to Wood Lake.

### Later phases and implementation considerations

The study identifies further design optimization, utility-conflict evaluation, permitting review, and, where applicable, agreements with private landowners or other public entities as work needed as a concept progresses. It also notes that the final configuration, cost, and functioning of project features may change during subsequent design phases.

For any Wilson Pond concept, the study assumes sufficient downstream capacity to route additional flow away from Richfield, which may need to be conveyed through the City of Bloomington or along the Highway 494 corridor to the Minnesota River. This routing was not included in the planning-level cost estimates. Further coordination and permitting discussions with the City of Bloomington or MnDOT would be required if the City of Richfield further evaluates a Wilson Pond concept.

The Near Woodlawn Terrace underground-storage concept would require an agreement with the owner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments.

[Information needed: Confirm the later phases planned for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Partners and roles

The available study was prepared for the City of Richfield by Barr Engineering Co. City staff reviewed the flood-risk-area prioritization and identified the three locations for planning-level evaluation. The study does not assign delivery responsibilities for a selected grant project.

[Information needed: Provide the delivery roles of each partner for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

title: Project analysis
body_markdown:
## Project analysis

The City of Richfield's August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Identification and Prioritization* study provides a planning-level alternatives assessment for six flood-risk mitigation concepts at Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace. The application project has not been selected from these concepts; therefore, project-specific conclusions on alternatives, feasibility, effects, review, and public engagement cannot yet be confirmed.

[Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept that this Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application will fund.]

### Alternatives and modeled effectiveness

The study's prioritization framework considered storm-system conditions, critical infrastructure, frequency of flooding, social vulnerability index, and the number of flood-prone structures. City staff selected three flood-risk areas for planning-level evaluation: Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace.

The available alternatives are:

- **Wilson Pond Concept A:** Lower the Wilson Pond water level ahead of a storm event, lower outlet and downstream storm-sewer inverts, and increase storm-sewer capacity toward Highway 494.
- **Wilson Pond Concept B:** Replace the downstream storm sewer from Wilson Pond to Highway 494 with a single 5-foot-by-5-foot box culvert.
- **Wilson Pond Concept C:** Increase the number and size of downstream storm-sewer pipes from Wilson Pond to Highway 494 through two parallel 5-foot-by-5-foot box culverts.
- **Northwest of Roosevelt Park Concept A:** Add an underground storage chamber beneath the Roosevelt Park baseball fields, divert drainage from Roosevelt Park and along 76th Street, and modify storm-sewer connections.
- **Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept A:** Add an underground storage chamber beneath the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments, regrade the parking lot, and modify storm-sewer connections.
- **Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept B:** Increase storm-sewer capacity from the northwest corner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments to Wood Lake.

For Wilson Pond Concept A, the model indicates lower peak water levels of 1.9 feet at Wilson Pond, 0.1 feet upstream at East 73rd Street and South 17th Avenue, and 4.2 feet downstream at East 75th Street and South 15th Avenue during the 2-year, 24-hour event. During the 10-year, 24-hour event, the corresponding reductions are 1.4 feet, 0.8 feet, and 3.9 feet. During the 100-year, 24-hour event, the reduction is 0.3 feet at each of the three reported locations.

For the Northwest of Roosevelt Park underground-storage concept, modeled peak water levels are lower by 4.6 feet at the baseball fields, 2.2 feet upstream at 76th Street and South Clinton Avenue, and 0.4 feet downstream at 76th Street and South 3rd Avenue during the 2-year, 24-hour event. The reported reductions during the 10-year, 24-hour event are 3.7 feet, 1.0 foot, and 0.5 feet, respectively; during the 100-year, 24-hour event, they are 0.7 feet, 0.5 feet, and 0.7 feet, respectively.

For Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept B, modeled peak water levels are lower by 1.1 feet in the parking lot within the flood-risk area, unchanged at Wood Lake, and lower by 0.3 feet at Lincoln Baseball Fields during the 2-year, 24-hour event. During the 10-year, 24-hour event, the reported reductions are 0.8 feet, 0.0 feet, and 0.5 feet, respectively; during the 100-year, 24-hour event, they are 1.1 feet, 0.0 feet, and 0.7 feet, respectively.

### Feasibility and implementation considerations

All alternatives in the study are concept-level designs. The study identifies the need for design optimization, utility-conflict evaluation, permitting review, and, where applicable, agreements with private landowners or other public entities before a concept is pursued.

The Wilson Pond alternatives would increase the volume and peak discharge rate leaving Richfield. They assume that additional flow can be routed from Highway 494 through the City of Bloomington or along the Highway 494 corridor to the Minnesota River. The routing beyond the municipal boundary has not been determined, is not included in the planning-level cost estimates, and would require further coordination and permitting discussions.

The Near Woodlawn Terrace underground-storage alternative would require an agreement with the owner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments. At Wilson Pond, surface storage was not considered because of limited undeveloped space near the flood-risk area and the City's direction not to consider property acquisition for flood-risk reduction. Underground storage was not considered there because groundwater is expected to be less than 10 feet below ground surface.

[Information needed: Provide the feasibility determination for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Environmental effects

The available planning study does not provide a project-specific environmental-effects assessment for a selected grant project. It identifies potential permitting requirements and site-specific considerations for further review as design advances.

[Information needed: Provide the environmental-effects assessment for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Social and economic effects

The study used the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index as a prioritization criterion. It describes social vulnerability as a measure of a community's ability to respond to a natural disaster and identifies Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace as areas with high social vulnerability index values. The study also identifies modeled exposure of residential structures, high-density housing, critical transportation routes, and a school at the evaluated locations.

These are planning-study indicators and do not establish the social or economic effects of the project to be selected for this application.

[Information needed: Provide the social and economic effects assessment for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Public input

The study states that Barr consulted with the City to identify flood-risk prioritization criteria, and City staff provided the scoring and weighting for those criteria. It does not document public input for a selected grant project.

[Information needed: Describe public input completed for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Environmental review

The available planning study does not state the environmental-review status for a selected grant project.

[Information needed: Confirm the environmental-review status for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Local water-plan alignment

The available planning study does not cite a local water-management plan or identify the plan provision with which a selected grant project aligns.

[Information needed: Provide the local water-management plan reference supporting the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Wetland-replacement-credit intent

The available planning study does not state whether the selected grant project will seek wetland-replacement credits.

title: Project financing
body_markdown:
## Project financing

The available August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Prioritization* study provides planning-level opinions of probable construction cost for six potential flood-risk mitigation concepts. It does not identify the concept to be funded, the current project phase, a financing method, committed funding sources, or the City of Richfield's financial capability for the selected project.

### Available planning-level cost information

The planning-level cost estimates are presented in 2025 U.S. dollars and have an estimated accuracy range of -30% to +50%. They are concept-level opinions of probable construction cost and do not include time escalation, base planning, engineering and design, construction management, permitting, property or easement acquisition, operations and maintenance, or monitoring. A 25% contingency is included in the estimated construction costs for ancillary items not separately quantified at this stage.

| Potential mitigation concept | Planning-level construction cost estimate |
| --- | ---: |
| Wilson Pond Concept A — reduce the water level in Wilson Pond ahead of a storm event and modify the outlet by lowering the invert and increasing storm-sewer capacity | $8,853,000 ($6,198,000–$15,493,000) |
| Wilson Pond Concept B — increase storm-sewer capacity | $11,536,000 ($8,076,000–$20,188,000) |
| Wilson Pond Concept C — increase storm-sewer capacity and number of pipes | $17,333,000 ($12,134,000–$30,333,000) |
| Northwest of Roosevelt Park Concept A — add an underground storage chamber | $15,491,000 ($10,844,000–$27,110,000) |
| Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept A — add an underground storage chamber | $1,540,000 ($1,078,000–$2,695,000) |
| Near Woodlawn Terrace Concept B — increase storm-sewer capacity | $7,440,000 ($5,208,000–$13,020,000) |

The final cost of a selected concept may change with further investigation, optimization, and detailed design. For Wilson Pond concepts, the planning-level estimates also do not include routing additional flow beyond Richfield's municipal boundary.
